objectives.title: Recognize how data is organized in everyday situations
Distinguish an abstract data type from a data structure
Describe common collections and their rules
Name the main ideas of object-oriented programming
Explain encapsulation and access control in a class

chunks.text: People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.

Libraries shelve books by call number, so a reader can walk to the right shelf instead of checking every book. A family tree shows how relatives are connected across generations. A subway map shows stations and the lines that join them.

An abstract data type (ADT) is a description of a kind of data and the operations allowed on it, for example add, remove, and contains. An ADT says what the operations do. It does not say how the data is kept in memory, and it does not depend on a programming language.

A data structure is a concrete way to store data in a program, written in a specific language. It implements the operations of an ADT. The same ADT can have several data structures behind it, such as an array-based version and a linked version.
Separating the ADT from the data structure lets a programmer change the storage later without changing the code that only uses the operations.
A collection is an ADT that holds a group of items. Collections differ in two rules: whether the same item may appear more than once, and whether the items are kept in a particular order.
A bag holds items in no particular order and allows duplicates. A set holds items in no particular order and does not allow duplicates. A list keeps items in a sequence, and each item has a position.

A stack adds and removes items at the same end, so the last item added is the first removed (LIFO). A queue adds items at the back and removes them from the front, so the first item added is the first removed (FIFO). A map stores pairs of a key and a value and finds a value by its key.

In object-oriented programming a program is built from objects. A class is the blueprint, and each object is one instance of a class with its own data. The three main ideas covered here are encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.

Inheritance lets a new class, the subclass, reuse the fields and methods of an existing class. The subclass can add methods or override inherited ones. A subclass object is also an object of its parent class: a Dog is an Animal.
Polymorphism means code written for a parent type works with objects of any of its subclasses. When the code calls a method, the version defined by the actual object's class runs.

Encapsulation puts an object's data and the methods that use that data together in one class, and keeps the data from being changed directly from outside. In Java the fields are usually declared private, and other code works with the object through public methods.
A getter is a public method that returns the value of a private field. A setter is a public method that changes a field, and it can check the new value first, for example rejecting a negative price.

A vending machine is a good picture of encapsulation. Buyers use only the buttons and the coin slot. The coin counter and the motors stay inside the case, and the owner can replace them without changing how buyers use the machine.
